Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $V$ be a real or complex vector space with a norm $\|\cdot\|$. Then $\|\cdot\|$ is induced by an inner product on $V$ if and only if it satisfies the parallelogram law

$$\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2 \qquad (x,y\in V).$$

In that case the inner product is unique, and it is given by the real polarisation formula

$$\langle x,y\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2\bigr)$$

in the real case, and by the complex polarisation formula

$$\langle x,y\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2+i\|x+iy\|^2-i\|x-iy\|^2\bigr)$$

in the complex case with the first-variable-linear convention.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces and let
$V:H\to K$ be a linear isometry. Then $V^\dagger V=I_H$. If $V$ is also
surjective, then $VV^\dagger=I_K$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

derivations.claim:
Put $C=T+sI_K$ and $P=V^\dagger TV+sI_H$. The operator $C$ is self-adjoint and $\langle Cz,zangle=\langle Tz,zangle+s\|z\|^2>0$ for $z
e0$. The adjoint identity [F8] and self-adjointness of $T$ give $\langle Pw,wangle=\langle TVw,Vwangle+s\|w\|^2>0$ for $w
e0$, since [F4] gives $Vw
e0$; the same adjoint identities show $P$ is self-adjoint. Thus both are normal by [F3] and positive definite by [F2]; [F7] diagonalizes each with strictly positive eigenvalues, so both inverses in the Statement exist.

For any positive-definite self-adjoint $C$ and any $y$, expansion using [F1] gives
$$2\operatorname{Re}\langle y,z\rangle-\langle Cz,z\rangle=\langle C^{-1}y,y\rangle-\langle C(z-C^{-1}y),z-C^{-1}y\rangle.$$
The last term is nonnegative and vanishes at $z=C^{-1}y$, hence $\langle C^{-1}y,y\rangle=\max_z(2\operatorname{Re}\langle y,z\rangle-\langle Cz,z\rangle)$.

Fix $x,w\in H$. By [F4]–[F5], the isometry preserves inner products, so $\langle Vx,Vw\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle$; [F6] gives $V^\dagger V=I_H$. Now apply step 2.1 to $y=Vx$ and $C=T+sI_K$, restricting the maximum to $z=Vw$. The restricted objective equals $2\operatorname{Re}\langle x,w\rangle-\langle Pw,w\rangle$. Maximizing over $w$ and applying step 2.1 to $P$ yields $\langle (T+sI_K)^{-1}Vx,Vx\rangle\ge\langle P^{-1}x,x\rangle$. Since this holds for every $x$, the difference of the two self-adjoint operators has nonnegative quadratic form, which is exactly the asserted operator order.

derivations.claim: For $x>0$ and $0<a<b$, direct integration gives $\int_a^b((x+s)^{-1}-(1+s)^{-1})\,ds=\ln(x+b)-\ln(1+b)-\ln(x+a)+\ln(1+a)$. Taking $a\downarrow0$ and $b\to\infty$ gives $-\ln x$. The spectra of $T$ and $V^\dagger TV$ lie in compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$ by [F2] and positive definiteness, so applying this scalar identity to their finite spectral decompositions gives the corresponding operator-norm integral formula for each.

For $0<a<b$, apply [F1] for each $s\in[a,b]$ and integrate the nonnegative operator difference. The scalar term $(1+s)^{-1}I$ cancels under compression because [F4] gives $V^\dagger V=I_H$. Thus
$$V^\dagger\!\int_a^b\!((T+sI_K)^{-1}-(1+s)^{-1}I_K)\,ds\,V-\int_a^b\!((V^\dagger TV+sI_H)^{-1}-(1+s)^{-1}I_H)\,ds\succeq0.$$

The operator integrands are bounded near $s=0$ because both compressed and uncompressed operators have strictly positive smallest eigenvalue. For $s\ge1$, $(T+sI)^{-1}=s^{-1}I+O(s^{-2})$ and $(V^\dagger TV+sI)^{-1}=s^{-1}I+O(s^{-2})$ in operator norm by the finite spectral theorem; the $s^{-1}I$ terms cancel using [F4], leaving an integrable $O(s^{-2})$ difference. Hence the two truncated operators in step 2.1 converge in norm to $-\log T$ and $-\log(V^\dagger TV)$ as the cutoffs tend to $0$ and $+\infty$. Norm limits preserve nonnegative operator order because each quadratic form converges, proving the Statement.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

derivations.claim: Choose orthonormal eigenbases $(a_i)_i$ and $(b_j)_j$ with $Aa_i=\alpha_i a_i$ and $Bb_j=\beta_j b_j$, where all $\alpha_i,\beta_j>0$, using [F2]. Define $E_{ji}x=\langle x,a_i\rangle b_j$. The finite trace formula [F3] gives $\langle E_{ji},E_{\ell k}\rangle_{HS}=\delta_{j\ell}\delta_{ik}$, and the $E_{ji}$ span the endomorphisms, so they form an orthonormal basis for the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product. Moreover $\Delta_{B,A}(E_{ji})=B E_{ji} A^{-1}=(\beta_j/\alpha_i)E_{ji}$. Thus $\Delta_{B,A}$ is self-adjoint positive definite and its spectral logarithm acts on $E_{ji}$ by $\ln(\beta_j/\alpha_i)$.

With the stated first-linear convention, the coefficient is $c_{ji}=\langle A^{1/2},E_{ji}\rangle_{HS}=\sqrt{\alpha_i}\langle a_i,b_j\rangle$, so $|c_{ji}|^2=\alpha_i|\langle a_i,b_j\rangle|^2$. Therefore the left side in the Statement is $\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i|\langle a_i,b_j\rangle|^2\ln(\alpha_i/\beta_j)$. Summing first over $j$ in the $\ln\alpha_i$ term gives $\operatorname{tr}(A\log A)$ by completeness of $(b_j)$; summing first over $i$ in the $\ln\beta_j$ term gives $\operatorname{tr}(A\log B)$ by expanding each $b_j$ in the $A$ eigenbasis. Their difference is $D(A\Vert B)$ by [F1], proving the identity.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and write $\mathcal L(H)$ and $\mathcal L(K)$ for their vector spaces of complex-linear endomorphisms with pointwise operations ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], [[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]]). Let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. For each integer $r\ge1$, put $R=\mathbb C^r$ with its standard ordered register basis ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). Write an operator $X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes R)$ in its unique $r\times r$ block form $X=[X_{ij}]$ with $X_{ij}\in\mathcal L(H)$, and define $\Phi^{(r)}(X)$ to have blocks $[\Phi(X_{ij})]$ on $K\otimes R$. Lemma [[lem-qc-finite-ancilla-amplification-is-block-map]] proves that this block rule defines a linear map on the full operator space for every finite $r$. For $r=1$, the extension is $\Phi$ under the canonical unitary identifications $x\mapsto x\otimes e_0$ and $y\mapsto y\otimes e_0$ proved in that lemma.

The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** if, for every finite $r\ge1$, $\Phi^{(r)}$ sends every nonnegative operator on $H\otimes R$ to a nonnegative operator on $K\otimes R$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]). The quantifier includes $r=1$; complete positivity therefore implies positivity. No Kraus, Choi, or Stinespring characterization is part of this definition.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

derivations.claim: For each $y$, [F1] makes $M_y$ nonnegative and self-adjoint, and [F3] makes it normal; [F2] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_{yj})_j$. Each eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_{yj}=\langle M_yu_{yj},u_{yj}\rangle\ge0$. Define $K_{yj}:H\to K$ by $K_{yj}x=\sqrt{\lambda_{yj}}\langle x,u_{yj}\rangle|y\rangle$. The family is finite and $K_{yj}^\dagger K_{yj}=\lambda_{yj}|u_{yj}\rangle\langle u_{yj}|$.

For every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, the diagonal output entry at $y$ of $\sum_{y,j}K_{yj}XK_{yj}^\dagger$ is $\sum_j\lambda_{yj}\langle Xu_{yj},u_{yj}\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(M_yX)$, while every off-diagonal outcome entry is $0$. Thus this finite Kraus sum is exactly $\mathcal M(X)$, so $\mathcal M$ is complex-linear. Moreover $\sum_{y,j}K_{yj}^\dagger K_{yj}=\sum_yM_y=I_H$ by [F1]. By [F7], $\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal M(X))=\sum_{y,j}\operatorname{tr}(K_{yj}XK_{yj}^\dagger)=\operatorname{tr}(X\sum_{y,j}K_{yj}^\dagger K_{yj})=\operatorname{tr}(X)$ for every $X$.

Fix any finite ancillary dimension $r\ge1$ and any nonnegative $Q\in\mathcal L(H\otimes\mathbb C^r)$. The product inner product and [F6] give $(K_{yj}\otimes I_r)^\dagger=K_{yj}^\dagger\otimes I_r$ by checking the adjoint pairing on elementary tensors and extending linearly. The amplified map is therefore $\mathcal M^{(r)}(Q)=\sum_{y,j}(K_{yj}\otimes I_r)Q(K_{yj}^\dagger\otimes I_r)$. Each summand is nonnegative because its quadratic form at $z$ is $\langle Q(K_{yj}^\dagger\otimes I_r)z,(K_{yj}^\dagger\otimes I_r)z\rangle\ge0$. Hence every amplification preserves nonnegativity, and [F4] makes $\mathcal M$ completely positive. Complex-linearity, complete positivity, and trace preservation give the channel conclusion by [F5].

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $n\ge1$, let $A_i,B_i:H\to H$ be non-negative for $1\le i\le n$, and let $\lambda_i\ge0$ with $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. Then, in the extended-real order,

$$D\!\left(\sum_i\lambda_iA_i\,\middle\|\,\sum_i\lambda_iB_i\right)\le\sum_i\lambda_iD(A_i\|B_i),$$

where zero-weight terms are omitted from the right side, and the order is that on the extended real line.

Let $V:H\to K$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces satisfying $V^*V=I_H$, and let $A,B$ be non-negative on $H$. Then

$$D(VAV^*\|VBV^*)=D(A\|B).$$

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with $d=\dim K\ge1$, and fix an ordered orthonormal basis $e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1}$ of $K$. Let $X e_j=e_{j+1\,\mathrm{mod}\,d}$ and $Z e_j=\omega^j e_j$, where $\omega=\exp(2\pi i/d)$ (and $\omega=1$ when $d=1$). For $R\in\operatorname{End}(H\otimes K)$,
$$\frac1{d^2}\sum_{p,q=0}^{d-1}(I_H\otimes X^pZ^q)R(I_H\otimes X^pZ^q)^\dagger=(\operatorname{Tr}_K R)\otimes I_K/d.$$

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

derivations.claim: Let $U_{pq}=I_H\otimes X^pZ^q$ from [F4], and let $\mathcal T(R)=d^{-2}\sum_{p,q}U_{pq}RU_{pq}^\dagger$. The Weyl proof in [F4] verifies that every $X^pZ^q$ is unitary, so each $U_{pq}$ and each conjugate $U_{pq}AU_{pq}^\dagger$, $U_{pq}BU_{pq}^\dagger$ is respectively unitary or positive semidefinite. Their finite averages are positive semidefinite as well. By [F4], $\mathcal T(A)=C\otimes I_K/d$ and $\mathcal T(B)=D\otimes I_K/d$, where $C=\operatorname{Tr}_K A$ and $D=\operatorname{Tr}_K B$; positivity of these tensor products implies $C,D$ are positive semidefinite by evaluating on $x\otimes e$ for a unit vector $e\in K$.

For any positive semidefinite $C,D$ on $H$, support inclusion for $(C,D)$ is equivalent to support inclusion for $(C\otimes I_K/d,D\otimes I_K/d)$ because $I_K/d$ is positive definite and its support is all of $K$. In the finite branch, spectral calculus on the product basis gives $\ln(C\otimes I_K/d)=(\ln C)\otimes I_K-(\ln d)I$ on its support, and the analogous formula for $D$. The product-basis trace factors as $\operatorname{tr}(R\otimes S)=\operatorname{tr}(R)\operatorname{tr}(S)$, since its diagonal entries are all products of the diagonal entries of $R$ and $S$. Since $\operatorname{tr}(I_K/d)=1$, this gives $$\operatorname{tr}((C\otimes I_K/d)\ln(C\otimes I_K/d))=\operatorname{tr}(C\ln C)-(\ln d)\operatorname{tr}(C),$$ $$\operatorname{tr}((C\otimes I_K/d)\ln(D\otimes I_K/d))=\operatorname{tr}(C\ln D)-(\ln d)\operatorname{tr}(C).$$ The scalar terms cancel in their difference, giving $D(C\otimes I_K/d\Vert D\otimes I_K/d)=D(C\Vert D)$. If support inclusion fails, both sides are $+\infty$ by [F1].

Apply [F2] to the uniform finite family of conjugate pairs and then [F3] to each unitary $U_{pq}$. The result is $$D(C\otimes I_K/d\Vert D\otimes I_K/d)=D(\mathcal T(A)\Vert\mathcal T(B))\le d^{-2}\sum_{p,q}D(U_{pq}AU_{pq}^\dagger\Vert U_{pq}BU_{pq}^\dagger)=D(A\Vert B).$$ The inequality is in the extended real order, so it also holds if the right side is $+\infty$.
Substitute the C,D from step 1.1 into step 1.2 and then use step 2.1. This yields $D(\operatorname{Tr}_K A\Vert\operatorname{Tr}_K B)\le D(A\Vert B)$, as required.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be a quantum channel. It has a finite
Kraus representation, and for any chosen such representation with $N$
operators $K_a:H\to K$ there are an $N$-dimensional environment $E$ and a
linear isometry $V:H\to K\otimes E$ such that
$$\Phi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^\dagger)\quad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

Let $H,K$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with $d=\dim K\ge1$, and let $A,B$ be positive semidefinite endomorphisms of $H\otimes K$. Then
$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_K A\Vert\operatorname{Tr}_K B)\le D(A\Vert B),$$
with the extended support convention.

Let $V:H\to K$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces satisfying $V^*V=I_H$, and let $A,B$ be non-negative on $H$. Then

$$D(VAV^*\|VBV^*)=D(A\|B).$$

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

derivations.claim: The channel hypothesis has the complete-positivity and trace-preservation content in [F5], so the finite Stinespring theorem [F2] gives an environment $E$ and isometry $V:H\to K\otimes E$ with $\Phi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^\dagger)$ for every $X$. Since $H\ne\{0\}$, $E$ is nonzero: otherwise $K\otimes E=\{0\}$ and no isometry from $H$ could exist.

Apply partial-trace data processing [F3] to the pair $VAV^\dagger,VBV^\dagger$ on $K\otimes E$, then use [F2] to identify their partial traces with $\Phi(A),\Phi(B)$ and [F4] to identify the input divergence. The support convention [F1] supplies the extended order if the input divergence is $+\infty$. Thus $$D(\Phi(A)\Vert\Phi(B))=D(\operatorname{Tr}_E(VAV^\dagger)\Vert\operatorname{Tr}_E(VBV^\dagger))\le D(VAV^\dagger\Vert VBV^\dagger)=D(A\Vert B).$$ All inequalities use the extended order, so the case $D(A\Vert B)=+\infty$ is included without subtracting infinite quantities.
